If the interaction is significant, we should be cautious in interpreting the main effects, as they may not represent the overall effects across all levels of the other factor. If the interaction is not significant, we can consider removing it from the model and interpreting the main effects directly. Let’s check the interaction plot to visualize the interaction effect. ggplot(tt, aes(x = dose, y = len, color = supp, group = supp)) + geom_point(position = position_dodge(0.2)) + geom_line(position = position_dodge(0.2)) + labs(title = "Interaction Plot: Tooth Length by Dose and Supplement Type", x = "Dose (mg)", y = "Tooth Length (mm)") It appears that OJ at doses 0.5 and 1.0 results in longer tooth lengths compared to VC, but at dose 2.0, both supplements yield similar tooth lengths. It can be hard to interpret so much output, and we also need to be careful about multiple comparisons. Let’s suppose that our research question is: “how do the dose level effects differ by supplement type?” We can use emmeans to answer this specific question. emm <- emmeans(mod2, ~ dose | supp) pairs(emm) ## supp = OJ: ## contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value ## dose0.5 - dose1 -9.47 1.62 54 -5.831 <.0001 ## dose0.5 - dose2 -12.83 1.62 54 -7.900 <.0001 ## dose1 - dose2 -3.36 1.62 54 -2.069 0.1060 ## ## supp = VC: ## contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value ## dose0.5 - dose1 -8.79 1.62 54 -5.413 <.0001 ## dose0.5 - dose2 -18.16 1.62 54 -11.182 <.0001 ## dose1 - dose2 -9.37 1.62 54 -5.770 <.0001 ## ## P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates This indicates that tooth growth increases with dose for both supplement types, but for OJ the increase is not significant from dose 1 to dose 2, while for VC the increase is significant at each step. To improve this, we might only want to test the increase in dosages from 0.5 to 1 and from 1 to 2, because the increase from 0.5 to 2 is redundant. We can do this by specifying contrasts in emmeans. contrast(emm, method = "trt.vs.ctrl", by = "supp", adjust = "holm") ## supp = OJ: ## contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value ## dose1 - dose0.5 9.47 1.62 54 5.831 <.0001 ## dose2 - dose0.5 12.83 1.62 54 7.900 <.0001 ## ## supp = VC: ## contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value ## dose1 - dose0.5 8.79 1.62 54 5.413 <.0001 ## dose2 - dose0.5 18.16 1.62 54 11.182 <.0001 ## ## P value adjustment: holm method for 2 tests In this case, we note that contrast chooses the base level of the factor as the control group. So for dose, the control is 0.5, and we are testing 1 vs 0.5 and 2 vs 0.5. The Holm adjustment is a way to control the family-wise error rate when making multiple comparisons. If we wanted to test 0.5 vs 1 and 1 vs 2 instead, we would need to reorder the levels of the factor dose so that 1 is the base level. This is not really treatment vs control, but the function is flexible enough to handle this situation. 8.4.2 Penguins Let’s do one more ANOVA. Suppose we want to model body_mass on species and sex. Twenty-four participants read 60 sentences and agreed to rate the accent of other participants (and themselves) on a scale of 1-6, with lower being better. The data set contains 5760 observations; not every participant rated every combination of participant and sentence. In this example, we are only interested in the reaction time of the rater. In particular, we are interested in whether the mean reaction time is different when the participant listens to themselves. We point out that there are many things going on in this data! We have the speakers repeating, we have the sentences repeating, and we have the same participant rating 240 sentences. In this first example, we are going to ignore the possible dependence on sentences and speakers, and focus only on the possible dependence on rater. It seems likely that each rater has their own mean time for rating, rather than all of the raters having the same overall mean time for rating. Let’s look at a plot. aa <- ardata::accent ggplot(aa, aes(x = factor(pp), y = rt, color = voice)) + geom_boxplot() We see some other issues that come up in this plot - reaction time is right skew, and we don’t appear to have equal variances across groups. Nonetheless, we continue. We also note that some of the reaction times are suspiciously small. aa |> slice_min(rt, n = 10) ## # A tibble: 10 × 15 ## pair pp group sentence spk_thisTrial voice wavfile trial rating rt ## <fct> <int> <fct> <int> <int> <fct> <fct> <int> <int> <dbl> ## 6 23_26 23 B 16 26 other spk26_16… 144 1 0.00258 ## 7 7_25 7 A 13 25 other spk25_13… 213 6 0.00261 ## 8 10_8 10 C 2 8 other spk8_2.w… 159 3 0.00357 ## 9 2_2 2 D 39 2 self spk2_39.… 172 2 0.0171 ## 10 20_2 20 D 9 2 other spk2_9.w… 94 3 0.0176 ## # ℹ 5 more variables: participant <int>, voiceC <dbl>, trialC <dbl>, ## # recognition <dbl>, simRatingPair <dbl> Let’s remove any of the data that has a reaction time less than 0.2 seconds, which already seems very fast. aa <- aa |> filter(rt > 0.2) The model that we will use is6 \[\begin{equation} \text{RT}_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + \beta_1 \text{Voice}_{ij} + u_{0i} + \epsilon_{ij} \tag{8.1} \end{equation}\] where: \(\text{RT}_{ij}\) is the reaction time for participant \(i\) on observation \(j\) \(\gamma_{00}\) is the mean RT when rating self voice (the reference category) \(\beta_1\) is the difference in mean RT between rating other voices and self voice \(u_{0i} \sim N(0, \tau^2)\) represents between-participant variance \(\epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) represents within-participant variance \(u_{0i}\) and \(\epsilon_{ij}\) are assumed to be independent Interpretation: Each person’s reaction time is a function of: The mean RT for self voice (\(\gamma_{00}\)) The difference in RT between other and self voice (\(\beta_1\)), which is constant across all participants That person’s individual baseline deviation (\(u_{0i}\)), which varies randomly across participants Random measurement error (\(\epsilon_{ij}\)) The key feature of this model is that it allows each participant to have their own baseline reaction time (random intercept) while estimating a common effect of voice type across all participants. We can estimate these values using lme4::lmer. library(lme4) ## Loading required package: Matrix ## ## Attaching package: 'Matrix' ## The following objects are masked from 'package:tidyr': ## ## expand, pack, unpack aa <- aa |> mutate(pp = factor(pp)) mod <- lme4::lmer(rt ~ voice + (1|pp), data = aa) summary(mod) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: rt ~ voice + (1 | pp) ## Data: aa ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 16395.8 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -2.6393 -0.5944 -0.1898 0.3646 9.6171 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## pp (Intercept) 0.3176 0.5636 ## Residual 1.0892 1.0437 ## Number of obs: 5572, groups: pp, 24 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. Error t value ## (Intercept) 1.45519 0.11617 12.526 ## voiceself -0.02736 0.03227 -0.848 ## ## Correlation of Fixed Effects: ## (Intr) ## voiceself -0.070 Make sure you can match the output to the model above. In particular, note that the intercept is the mean RT for self voice, and the coefficient for voiceother is the difference in mean RT between other and self voice. The variance components tell us: - \(\hat{\tau}^2 = 0.3354\) (between-participant variance): Participants vary substantially in their baseline RT - \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = 1.0888\) (within-participant variance): There’s also considerable variation within each participant’s ratings - ICC = \(\frac{\hat{\tau}^2}{\hat{\tau}^2 + \hat{\sigma}^2} \approx 0.235\) indicates that approximately 23.5% of the total variance in RT is attributable to differences between participants, while the remaining 76.5% is due to within-participant variation (e.g., differences across sentences, speakers, and random error). This justifies our use of random intercepts for participants. Let’s also assess the normality of the residuals. plot(mod) qqnorm(resid(mod)) qqline(resid(mod)) As you can see, we have significant skewness and heteroskedasticity. One way to try to help that is by replacing reaction time with its log. mod <- lme4::lmer(log(rt) ~ voice + (1|pp), data = aa) #here it is good we removed very small values summary(mod) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: log(rt) ~ voice + (1 | pp) ## Data: aa ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 10836.6 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -3.4587 -0.6703 0.0208 0.6994 3.5437 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## pp (Intercept) 0.1114 0.3338 ## Residual 0.4016 0.6337 ## Number of obs: 5572, groups: pp, 24 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. This is a good way to check our understanding of the model and the estimation process. If you can do this reliably with all of the models we cover in this class, you will be in a very good position to understand the models and to apply them to your own data. Recall that we had the following model (before taking logs): library(lme4) aa <- ardata::accent |> mutate(pp = factor(pp)) mod <- lme4::lmer(rt ~ voice + (1|pp), data = aa) summary(mod) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: rt ~ voice + (1 | pp) ## Data: aa ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 16945.1 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -2.6414 -0.6020 -0.1848 0.3715 9.6194 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## pp (Intercept) 0.3354 0.5791 ## Residual 1.0888 1.0434 ## Number of obs: 5760, groups: pp, 24 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. Error t value ## (Intercept) 1.42074 0.11927 11.912 ## voiceself -0.02617 0.03175 -0.824 ## ## Correlation of Fixed Effects: ## (Intr) ## voiceself -0.067 Let’s simulate the data. It is nice to be able to read the estimates from the table by eye or to do it by code. Let’s do it by code, which is more reliable, and check our understanding by looking at the values and making sure they match what we think it should. gamma <- summary(mod)$coefficients["(Intercept)", "Estimate"] gamma ## [1] 1.420738 beta <- summary(mod)$coefficients["voiceself", "Estimate"] beta ## [1] -0.02616764 tau <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mod))$vcov[1] #between-participant variance tau #NOTE: we will have to take square root of this inside of rnorm! ## [1] 0.3353698 sigma <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mod))$vcov[2] #within-participant variance sigma #NOTE: we will have to take square root of this inside of rnorm! ## [1] 1.088765 We pause here to note that these are all of the parameters of the model. The values of \(u_i\) are not considered paramaters of the model; they are considered random effects, and we will simulate them as random draws from a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance \(\tau^2\). The values of \(\epsilon_{ij}\) are also not considered parameters of the model; they are considered random errors, and we will simulate them as random draws from a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma^2\). Now we can simulate the data. We will simulate data for 24 participants, with 240 observations per participant, which is the same as in the original data set. Note that this simulation makes explicit that we do not model sentence or speaker at all. We are only modeling the dependence on pp (participant) and voice. u <- rnorm(24, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(tau)) #random intercepts for each participant n <- 24 * 240 #total number of observations sim_data <- data.frame(pp = factor(rep(1:24, each = 240)), voice = rep(c("self", "other"), times = c(180, 60))) #we assume 180 self ratings and 60 other ratings per participant, which is consistent with the original data set): head(table(aa$pp, aa$voice)) ## ## other self ## 1 180 60 ## 2 180 60 ## 3 180 60 ## 4 180 60 ## 5 180 60 ## 6 180 60 aa |> count(pp, voice) ## # A tibble: 48 × 3 ## pp voice n ## <fct> <fct> <int> ## 1 1 other 180 ## 2 1 self 60 ## 3 2 other 180 ## 4 2 self 60 ## 5 3 other 180 ## 6 3 self 60 ## 7 4 other 180 ## 8 4 self 60 ## 9 5 other 180 ## 10 5 self 60 ## # ℹ 38 more rows sim_data <- sim_data |> mutate(rt = gamma + beta * case_when(voice == "self" ~ 1, TRUE ~ 0) + u[as.numeric(pp)] + rnorm(n(), mean = 0, sd = sqrt(sigma)) ) lmerTest::lmer(rt ~ voice + (1|pp), data = sim_data) |> summary() ## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [ ## lmerModLmerTest] ## Formula: rt ~ voice + (1 | pp) ## Data: sim_data ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 17213.4 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -3.5917 -0.6549 -0.0131 0.6794 3.7931 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## pp (Intercept) 0.395 0.6285 ## Residual 1.140 1.0678 ## Number of obs: 5760, groups: pp, 24 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. This data set contains reaction times for 18 subjects who were sleep deprived for 10 days. We will model the reaction time as a function of the number of days of sleep deprivation, with random intercepts for each subject. Let’s look at the data. We can fit a regression line to the data, using the same slope but a different intercept for each subject. How do we do that? Try to do it yourself before looking at the code below. This is a good refresher for what we were doing earlier in the class. ss <- lme4::sleepstudy |> janitor::clean_names() model <- lm(reaction ~ days + subject, data = ss) pred <- broom::augment(model) model2 <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1|subject), data = ss) pred2 <- broom.mixed::augment(model2) # note: broom.mixed, not broom ggplot(pred, aes(x = days, y = .fitted, color = subject)) + geom_line(alpha = 0.8) + #geom_line(data = pred2, aes(x = days, y = .fitted, color = subject), alpha = 0.3) + #uncomment to see the random slopes labs(x = "Days", y = "Reaction") + geom_point(aes(y = reaction)) + theme_minimal() This would be fine if we were only interested in these subjects. More likely, though, we are imagining the subjects to be a random sample from a larger population, and we want to treat the intercept as a random effect and the slope as a fixed effect. This way, we can make inferences about the overall effect of days of sleep deprivation on reaction time, while accounting for the fact that each subject has their own baseline reaction time (random intercept). The model would be \[ \text{reaction}_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + \beta_1 \text{days}_{ij} + u_{0i} + \epsilon_{ij} \] where -\(\gamma_{00}\) is the mean reaction time for a subject with 0 days of sleep deprivation, -\(\beta_1\) is the fixed effect of days of sleep deprivation on reaction time -\(u_{0i} \sim N(0, \tau^2)\) represents the random intercept for subject \(i\) -\(\epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) represents the error term for observation \(j\) of subject \(i\) -\(\tau\) and \(\sigma\) are the variances of the random intercepts and the error term, respectively. -We assume independence between the random intercepts and the error term, and we also assume that the random intercepts are independent across subjects. In order to build such a model, we use lme4::lmer as follows: mod <- lme4::lmer(reaction ~ days + (1|subject), data = ss) summary(mod) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: reaction ~ days + (1 | subject) ## Data: ss ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 1786.5 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -3.2257 -0.5529 0.0109 0.5188 4.2506 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## subject (Intercept) 1378.2 37.12 ## Residual 960.5 30.99 ## Number of obs: 180, groups: subject, 18 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. Error t value ## (Intercept) 251.4051 9.7467 25.79 ## days 10.4673 0.8042 13.02 ## ## Correlation of Fixed Effects: ## (Intr) ## days -0.371 We see that \(\gamma_{00}\) is estimated to be 251.405, which is the mean reaction time for a subject with 0 days of sleep deprivation. The fixed effect of days of sleep deprivation on reaction time is estimated to be 10.467, which means that for each additional day of sleep deprivation, the reaction time increases by about 10.467 milliseconds on average, after accounting for the random intercepts for each subject. The variance of the random intercepts is estimated to be 1378.2, and the variance of the error term is estimated to be 960.5. The ICC ( Intraclass Correlation Coefficient) can be calculated as \(\frac{1378.2}{1378.2 + 960.5} \approx 0.59\), which indicates that about 59% of the total variance in reaction time is attributable to differences between subjects, while the remaining 41% is due to within-subject variation (e.g., differences across days and random error). ICC stands for Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, and it is a measure of the proportion of total variance that is attributable to between-group (or between-subject) variance in a mixed effects model. It ranges from 0 to 1, where a value close to 0 indicates that most of the variance is within groups (or subjects), while a value close to 1 indicates that most of the variance is between groups (or subjects). We also see that \(\hat \beta_1\) is significant (\(t = 13.02, \text{se} = 0.8042\)), which suggests that there is a significant association between days of sleep deprivation and reaction time, even after accounting for the random intercepts for each subject. Let’s check the residuals of our model: plot(mod) qqnorm(resid(mod)) qqline(resid(mod)) Well, the residuals appear approximately normal, but they also appear to have a U shape in the residuals vs fitted. We will examine that again when we consider random slopes as well as random intercepts. For now, we will continue with this model, which only has random intercepts. One characteristic of mixed effect models is that the estimates for the intercepts of individual subjects are “shrunk” towards the overall mean. This is because the model borrows strength from the other subjects to estimate the intercepts, which can lead to more accurate estimates, especially for subjects with fewer observations. This is known as “partial pooling” or “shrinkage”. The amount of shrinkage depends on the variance of the random intercepts and the number of observations for each subject. Subjects with more observations will have less shrinkage, while subjects with fewer observations will have more shrinkage. We can plot the fixed effect model and the random effect model on the same graph to illustrate this. pred2 <- broom.mixed::augment(mod) ggplot(pred, aes(x = days, y = .fitted, color = subject)) + geom_line(alpha = 0.8) + geom_line(data = pred2, aes(x = days, y = .fitted, color = subject), alpha = 0.3) + labs(x = "Days", y = "Reaction") + geom_point(aes(y = reaction)) + theme_minimal() We see that the random effects lines (which are lighter) have intercepts which are closer to the overall mean of all of the intercepts than the fixed effect line is. 8.6.3 Adding random slopes We continue with the sleepstudy data set in the lme4 package. Let’s look once more at a scatterplot with lines of best fit for each subject. ggplot(ss, aes(x = days, y = reaction, color = subject)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F) ## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x' Based on this plot, it seems that we have potentially different intercepts and slopes for each subject. Let’s fit a linear model with an interaction between days and subject. We will have 18 intercepts and 18 slopes, which is a lot of parameters to estimate with only 180 observations. Following what we had done before, we would be done with our modeling. Here are some issues: We have no way to predict the reaction time for a new subject that is not in our data set, because we have no estimate of the intercept or slope for that subject. How would we answer the following question: is reaction time associated with number of days of sleep deprivation? We could look at the overall F-test for the model, but that is not really testing the association between reaction time and days of sleep deprivation. It is testing whether there is an association between reaction time and days of sleep deprivation for each subject. We would like to be able to test the overall association between reaction time and days of sleep deprivation, while accounting for the fact that we have different intercepts and slopes for each subject. Based on the plot, it seems like for some subjects, the reaction time might be getting faster with more sleep deprivation. We have a lot of parameters in this model, which can lead to overfitting. We haven’t really talked much about overfitting in this class yet. But, when we are looking for a parsimonious model by variable selection, we are trying to avoid overfitting. In this case, we have a lot of parameters, and we are not really interested in the individual intercepts and slopes for each subject. We are more interested in the overall association between reaction time and days of sleep deprivation, while accounting for the fact that we have (possibly) different intercepts and slopes for each subject. What is wrong with forgetting that we have the same subjects, and running the following regression? #THIS IS NOT ADVISED mod_wrong <- lm(reaction ~ days, data = ss) summary(mod_wrong) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = reaction ~ days, data = ss) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -110.848 -27.483 1.546 26.142 139.953 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. It is treating each observation as independent, which is not the case. This can lead to underestimated standard errors and inflated type I error rates. We need a way to account for the fact that we have repeated measurements for each subject, and that the intercepts and slopes may vary by subject. This is where mixed models come in, which we will cover in the next lecture. 8.7 February 19 8.7.1 Random Slopes When we have one predictor with random intercepts and slopes, the model can be written like this: \[ y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + b_{0i} + b_{1i} x_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij} \] where \(b_{0i}\) is the random intercept for group \(i\), and \(b_{1i}\) is the random slope for predictor \(x\) in group \(i\). We assume that the random effects \((b_{0i}, b_{1i})\) are jointly normally distributed with mean 0 and covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), and that the errors \(\epsilon_{ij}\) are normally distributed with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma^2\). The random effects and errors are assumed to be independent of each other. Note that we could also combine the fixed effects with the random effects to say that the intercept has mean \(\beta_0\) and the slope has mean \(\beta_1\), together with the covariance informarion. We can fit the data by using lmer as follows: mod <- lme4::lmer(reaction ~ days + (1 + days|subject), data = ss) summary(mod) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: reaction ~ days + (1 + days | subject) ## Data: ss ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 1743.6 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -3.9536 -0.4634 0.0231 0.4634 5.1793 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. Corr ## subject (Intercept) 612.10 24.741 ## days 35.07 5.922 0.07 ## Residual 654.94 25.592 ## Number of obs: 180, groups: subject, 18 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. Error t value ## (Intercept) 251.405 6.825 36.838 ## days 10.467 1.546 6.771 ## ## Correlation of Fixed Effects: ## (Intr) ## days -0.138 We obtain the following estimates for the parameters of the model: \(\hat \beta_0 = 251.405\) (mean intercept across subjects) \(\hat \beta_1 = 10.467\) (mean slope across subjects) \(\hat \tau_0^2 = 612.1\) (variance of random intercepts) \(\hat \tau_1^2 = 35\) (variance of random slopes) \(\hat \sigma^2 = 654.94\) (variance of residuals) \(\hat \rho = 0.07\) (correlation between random intercepts and slopes) Note that this model has one additional parameter which we didn’t specify in our mathematical model above, which is the correlation between random intercepts and slopes. A positive value for this correlation indicates that subjects with higher baseline reaction times (higher random intercepts) tend to have steeper increases in reaction time with more days of sleep deprivation (higher random slopes), while a negative value would indicate the opposite. In this case, the correlation is close to zero, suggesting that there is little relationship between the random intercepts and slopes in this data set. If we want to fit a model that does not include the correlation, we can use the following: mod <- lme4::lmer(reaction ~ days + (1 + days||subject), data = ss) #the || syntax forces the correlation to be zero summary(mod) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: reaction ~ days + ((1 | subject) + (0 + days | subject)) ## Data: ss ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 1743.7 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -3.9626 -0.4625 0.0204 0.4653 5.1860 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## subject (Intercept) 627.57 25.051 ## subject.1 days 35.86 5.988 ## Residual 653.58 25.565 ## Number of obs: 180, groups: subject, 18 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. Error t value ## (Intercept) 251.405 6.885 36.513 ## days 10.467 1.560 6.712 ## ## Correlation of Fixed Effects: ## (Intr) ## days -0.184 There is very little change in the estimated parameter values. One interesting question that can be asked with a model with random slopes is: what proportion of subjects have a positive slope? In other words, what proportion of subjects have reaction times that increase with more days of sleep deprivation? We can answer this question by looking at the distribution of the random slopes. random_slopes <- ranef(mod)$subject$days #this gives us the random slope for each subject mean_slope <- fixef(mod)["days"] #this gives us the fixed effect slope #the total slope for each subject is the fixed effect slope plus the random slope for that subject total_slopes <- mean_slope + random_slopes total_slopes ## [1] 19.7907830 1.8681102 5.0794915 5.4986357 7.2733482 10.1587920 ## [7] 10.1800781 11.5832770 -0.4386895 19.0949087 11.7479752 17.2236923 ## [13] 7.3921504 13.9794982 11.3403373 15.4510769 9.4619922 11.7256896 What is our estimate of the total percentage of the total population that has a negative slope? We can use the normal distribution to answer this question, because the random slopes are assumed to be normally distributed. pnorm(0, mean = mean_slope, sd = sqrt(35)) #35 is the variance of the random slopes, so we take the square root to get the standard deviation ## [1] 0.03842239 We see that about 4 percent of the population is estimated to have a negative slope, which means that their reaction times decrease with more days of sleep deprivation. This is an interesting finding, and it highlights the importance of looking at the random effects in a mixed model, rather than just the fixed effects. The fixed effect tells us about the average effect across all subjects, but the random effects tell us about the variability in the effect across subjects. In this case, while the average effect of days of sleep deprivation on reaction time is positive, there is a small proportion of subjects for whom the effect is negative. What is a confidence interval for the main slope effect? We can use the standard error of the fixed effect slope to construct a confidence interval. The standard error is given in the summary output of the model, or we can use emmeans or lmerTest to get it. For example, we can compare the model with random slopes to the model without random slopes, or we can compare the model with random slopes and random intercepts to the model with only random intercepts. We can also compare the model with correlated random effects to the model with uncorrelated random effects. Let’s see how to do this in R. mod_random_slopes <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1 + days|subject), data = ss) mod_random_intercepts <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1|subject), data = ss) anova(mod_random_intercepts, mod_random_slopes) ## refitting model(s) with ML (instead of REML) ## Data: ss ## Models: ## mod_random_intercepts: reaction ~ days + (1 | subject) ## mod_random_slopes: reaction ~ days + (1 + days | subject) ## npar AIC BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) ## mod_random_intercepts 4 1802.1 1814.8 -897.04 1794.1 ## mod_random_slopes 6 1763.9 1783.1 -875.97 1751.9 42.139 2 7.072e-10 ## ## mod_random_intercepts ## mod_random_slopes *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 In general, the null hypothesis being tested is that all of the extra parameters in the larger model are zero versus at least one of the parameters is not zero. So, a \(p\)-value less than 0.05 is evidence that the larger model is a significantly better fit to the data than the smaller model, which suggests that at least one of the extra parameters in the larger model is not zero. In this case, we are testing whether the variance of the random slopes is zero, which is equivalent to testing whether the random slopes are necessary to explain the variability in the data. If we reject the null hypothesis, we can conclude that there is significant variability in the slopes across subjects, and that the model with random slopes fits significantly better than the model with only random intercepts. If we fail to reject the null hypothesis, we can conclude that there is not enough evidence to suggest that there is significant variability in the slopes across subjects, and that the model with only random intercepts may be sufficient to explain the variability in the data. We can also look at the AIC or BIC values for the two models, which are measures of model fit that penalize for the number of parameters in the model. The model with the lower AIC or BIC value is generally considered to be the better fitting model. In this case, we would expect the model with random slopes to have a lower AIC and BIC value than the model with only random intercepts, which would further support the conclusion that the model with random slopes fits significantly better than the model with only random intercepts. We conclude that the model with random slopes fits significantly better than the model with only random intercepts, which suggests that there is significant variability in the slopes across subjects. We can also compare the model with correlated random effects to the model with uncorrelated random effects. Now let’s compare the model with correlated random effects to the model with uncorrelated random effects. mod_correlated <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1 + days|subject), data = ss, REML = F) mod_uncorrelated <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1 + days||subject), data = ss, REML = F) anova(mod_uncorrelated, mod_correlated) ## Data: ss ## Models: ## mod_uncorrelated: reaction ~ days + (1 + days || subject) ## mod_correlated: reaction ~ days + (1 + days | subject) ## npar AIC BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) ## mod_uncorrelated 5 1762.0 1778.0 -876.00 1752.0 ## mod_correlated 6 1763.9 1783.1 -875.97 1751.9 0.0639 1 0.8004 The model with uncorrelated random effects fits significantly better than the model with correlated random effects, which suggests that there is not a significant correlation between the random intercepts and random slopes in this data set. This is consistent with the estimate of the correlation that we obtained from the model with correlated random effects, which was close to zero. When we have different fixed effects, we should not use REML = T to compare the models, because the fixed effects are different. Note that anova will fix this for us if we forget. mod <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1|subject), data = ss, REML = F) mod2 <- lmer(reaction ~ 1 + (1|subject), data = ss, REML = F) anova(mod2, mod) ## Data: ss ## Models: ## mod2: reaction ~ 1 + (1 | subject) ## mod: reaction ~ days + (1 | subject) ## npar AIC BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) ## mod2 3 1916.5 1926.1 -955.27 1910.5 ## mod 4 1802.1 1814.8 -897.04 1794.1 116.46 1 < 2.2e-16 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 The model with the fixed effect of days fits significantly better than the model with only a random intercept. We can re-run this with REML = T and see we get the same answer, with a message. mod <- lmer(reaction ~ days + (1|subject), data = ss, REML = T) mod2 <- lmer(reaction ~ 1 + (1|subject), data = ss, REML = T) anova(mod2, mod) ## refitting model(s) with ML (instead of REML) ## Data: ss ## Models: ## mod2: reaction ~ 1 + (1 | subject) ## mod: reaction ~ days + (1 | subject) ## npar AIC BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq) ## mod2 3 1916.5 1926.1 -955.27 1910.5 ## mod 4 1802.1 1814.8 -897.04 1794.1 116.46 1 < 2.2e-16 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 8.8 February 24 8.8.1 Beethoven Tempo Example In this example, we consider Beethoven symphony tempo data from a ppaer by Martin-Castro and Ucar7. Let’s remind ourselves how we might estimate the variance of the random intercept. modlm <- lm(tempo ~ 1 + conductor, data = bb2) var(c(0, coef(modlm)[2:36]) + coef(modlm)[1]) ## [1] 11.80086 #alternative method bb2 |> group_by(conductor) |> summarize(mean_tempo = mean(tempo)) |> summarize(between_var = var(mean_tempo)) #gives same result ## # A tibble: 1 × 1 ## between_var ## <dbl> ## 1 11.8 This estimate gives us a variance of nearly 12, which is quite large. This is a common issue when we have a small number of groups (in this case, conductors) and/or a small number of observations per group. In this case, we have 36 conductors and five observations per conductor for mark 84, which is not a lot of data to estimate the variance of the random intercepts. This is why we get a zero estimate for the variance of the random intercepts, which is likely not the true value, but rather an artifact of the limited data we have for this particular mark. Chapter 9 Maximum Likelihood Estimation 9.1 MLE for mixed models

Chapter 9 Maximum Likelihood Estimation Consider the problem of estimating a parameter in a model. For example, if we take a random sample from a normal distribution with unknown mean \(\mu\) and variance 1, what is a good estimator for \(\mu\)? I hope you immediately think of the sample mean \(\overline{x}\). How could we come to that decision systematically, though? And what if the parameter doesn’t have quite the same obvious interpretation as \(\mu\) from a normal distribution? We will use the method of maximum likelihood. Realistically, I should have talked about this long ago in class, but we are going to do it now. Given a probability density function \(f\) of a random variable \(X\), we can associate the value of \(f(x)\) with the relative likelihood that \(x\) is an observed value from \(X\). The values themselves don’t mean much, but if \(f(x) = 2f(y)\), then we can say that \(x\) is twice as likely as \(y\). If we have a single observation from \(X\) which is normally distributed with mean \(\mu\), the most likely outcome is the mean, \(\mu\). Now, we can turn the thought process upside down. Suppose we don’t know the value of \(\mu\), but we observe a single value \(x\). The value of \(\mu\) which makes \(x\) most likely is \(x\) itself8. Let’s check that really is true. like_fun <- function(mu) { dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = 1) } x <- 2 optimize(like_fun, interval = c(-8, 8), maximum = T) ## $maximum ## [1] 2.000015 ## ## $objective ## [1] 0.3989423 If you try a few more values of \(x\), you will see that indeed, this is the case. OK, but how would we do this if we have more than one value of \(x\)? We would then compute the likelihood function given all of the samples. If the samples are independent (a common assumption, but not the case in mixed models), then we can just multiply the separate pdfs together. Let’s see how to do it if we have a sample of size \(n = 4\) consisting of c(1, 2, 3, 4). like_fun <- function(mu) { prod(dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = 1)) } x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4) optimize(like_fun, interval = c(-8, 8), maximum = T) ## $maximum ## [1] 2.500003 ## ## $objective ## [1] 0.002079237 This works fine for small data sets, but when we have a lot of data, the product of the pdfs could get extermely small. It is better to minimze the negative of the log of the likelihood. We also have to change prod to sum. like_fun <- function(mu) { sum(dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = 1, log = T)) } x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4) optimize(like_fun, interval = c(-8, 8), maximum = T) ## $maximum ## [1] 2.5 ## ## $objective ## [1] -6.175754 OK, now what if we have two parameters that we need to estimate simultaneously? There are several things that need to change: We have to pass two parameters to our likelihood function instead of just one. We have to use optim instead of optimize We have to provide optim with a starting estimate. optim will only minimize, so we need to minimize negative likelihood, which is the same as maximizing positive likelihood. It works like this in the case we are estimating the mean and the standard deviation. x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4) like_fun <- function(par) { mu <- par[1] sigma <- par[2] -sum(dnorm(x, mu, sigma, log = T)) } optim(par = c(1, 1), fn = like_fun, lower = c(-Inf, 0.001), method = "L-BFGS-B") ## $par ## [1] 2.500001 1.118036 ## ## $value ## [1] 6.122041 ## ## $counts ## function gradient ## 14 14 ## ## $convergence ## [1] 0 ## ## $message ## [1] "CONVERGENCE: REL_REDUCTION_OF_F <= FACTR*EPSMCH" This works quite generally. If we have data between 0 and 1 and we wish to estimate the parameters associated with a beta distribution, we can do the following: set.seed(1) shapes <- sample(1:50, 2) data <- rbeta(30, shape1 = shapes[1], shape2 = shapes[2]) like_fun <- function(par) { shape1 <- par[1] shape2 <- par[2] -sum(dbeta(data, shape1, shape2, log = T)) } oo <- optim(par = c(1, 1), fn = like_fun, lower = c(-0.01, 0.01), method = "L-BFGS-B") oo ## $par ## [1] 5.252771 53.286377 ## ## $value ## [1] -57.80793 ## ## $counts ## function gradient ## 20 20 ## ## $convergence ## [1] 0 ## ## $message ## [1] "CONVERGENCE: REL_REDUCTION_OF_F <= FACTR*EPSMCH" Are estimates are 5.252771 for shape1 and 53.2863773 for shape2. If we have data that follows the model \[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i \] where \(\epsilon_i\) are iid \(N(0, \sigma)\) random variables, then it gets a little bit more complicated. We would do it like this. We suppose we want to estimate the parameters associated with modeling imu_top_speed_ms on stride_length_m in the data set ardata::running_speed. The main thing to notice is that the values of \(y_i\) are independent, normally distributed with mean \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). rr <- ardata::running_speed like_fun <- function(par) { beta0 <- par[1] beta1 <- par[2] sigma <- par[3] -sum(dnorm(rr$imu_top_speed_ms, beta0 + beta1 * rr$stride_length_m, sigma, log = T)) } oo <- optim(par = c(1, 1, 1), fn = like_fun, lower = c(-Inf, -Inf, 0.01), method = "L-BFGS-B") oo$par ## [1] 2.2157883 1.5566788 0.5272198 lm(imu_top_speed_ms ~ stride_length_m, data = rr) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = imu_top_speed_ms ~ stride_length_m, data = rr) ## ## Coefficients: ## (Intercept) stride_length_m ## 2.216 1.557 9.1 MLE for mixed models How does lmer estimate the parameters in our models? lmer uses maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to estimate the parameters of the model. The likelihood function is based on the assumption that the random effects and the residuals are normally distributed. The MLE approach finds the parameter values that maximize the likelihood of observing the data given the model. In practice, lmer uses two different algorithms for estimating the parameters. The one we will discuss is MLE. Let’s look at an example. library(tidyverse) ## ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ── ## ✔ dplyr 1.2.0 ✔ readr 2.1.5 ## ✔ forcats 1.0.0 ✔ stringr 1.5.1 ## ✔ ggplot2 4.0.0 ✔ tibble 3.3.0 ## ✔ lubridate 1.9.4 ✔ tidyr 1.3.1 ## ✔ purrr 1.1.0 ## ── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ── ## ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter() ## ✖ dplyr::lag() masks stats::lag() ## ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors ss <- lme4::sleepstudy |> janitor::clean_names() |> as_tibble() We estimate the parameters involved with a random intercepts model. We can use these values as starting points for the optimization algorithm that lmer uses to find the MLE estimates. Using our mathematical model of reaction, we can see that each response is a function of the fixed effects, the random effects, and the residuals. The distribution of a single response is \[ y_{ij} \sim N(\gamma_{00} + \beta_1 x_{ij}, \tau^2 + \sigma^2) \] where here we use the assumption that \(u_{0i} \sim N(0, \tau^2)\) and \(\epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) are independent. The likelihood function is the product of the probability density functions for each response, which is a function of the parameters \(\gamma_{00}\), \(\beta_1\), \(\tau^2\), and \(\sigma^2\). The MLE estimates are the values of these parameters that maximize the likelihood function. When we do this, we will maximize the log of the likelihood function, in order to keep values reasonably sized. #This isn't correct like <- function(par) { gamma <- par[1] beta <- par[2] tau2 <- par[3] sigma2 <- par[4] mu <- gamma + beta * ss$days var <- tau2 + sigma2 -sum(dnorm(ss$reaction, mean = mu, sd = sqrt(var), log = TRUE)) } like(c(295, 10.5, 1474, 961)) ## [1] 1021.136 oo <- optim(par = c(295, 10.5, 1474, 961), fn = like, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(-Inf, -Inf, 0, 0)) like(oo$par) ## [1] 950.1465 tidy_modlmer <- broom.mixed::tidy(mod_lmer) like(c(tidy_modlmer$estimate[1], tidy_modlmer$estimate[2], tidy_modlmer$estimate[3]^2, tidy_modlmer$estimate[4]^2)) ## [1] 950.2107 We can see that we don’t quite get the fully correct answer. This is because we haven’t correctly described the likelihood function for a mixed effect model. The likelihood function for a mixed effect model is more complicated than the one we wrote down above, because it allows correlation within subjects. The likelihood function for a mixed effect model is based on the joint distribution of the responses for each subject, which is a multivariate normal distribution with mean vector and covariance matrix that depend on the fixed effects and the random effects. While the marginal distribution of each response is normal, the joint distribution of the responses for each subject is multivariate normal with correlation between responses from the same subject. This is fundamentally different than what we were doing in the previous section, because now we have to compute the joint likelihood of the entire sample directly, rather than multiplying the likelihood of the samples together. How would that work for linear regression Let’s return to the same example we did earlier with running speed. We have to understand multivariate normal distributions to some extent, so here we go. The multivariate normal distribution is a generalization of the univariate normal distribution to multiple dimensions. Its parameters are a mean vector and a covariance matrix. The mean vector gives the expected value of each variable, while the covariance matrix gives the variance of each variable and the covariance between each pair of variables. In the following example, we will look at the joint distribution of \((X_1, X_2)\), so the length of the mean vector will be 2 and the covariance matrix will be \(2 \times 2\). Sigma <- matrix(c(3, 2, 2, 5), nrow = 2) eigen(Sigma) #this is a positive definite matrix, so it is a valid covariance matrix ## eigen() decomposition ## $values ## [1] 6.236068 1.763932 ## ## $vectors ## [,1] [,2] ## [1,] 0.5257311 -0.8506508 ## [2,] 0.8506508 0.5257311 library(mvtnorm) dat <- mvtnorm::rmvnorm(n = 1000, mean = c(1, 4), sigma = Sigma) dd <- data.frame(dat) library(tidyverse) ggplot(dd, aes(x = X1, y = X2)) + geom_point() + coord_equal() To force independence of the coordinates, we set the covariances equal to zero. Note that for general rvs, uncorrelated does not imply independent, but for multivariate normal rvs, uncorrelated does imply independent. We can also re-estimate the mean vector and the covariance matrix using MLE as follows: like_fun <- function(par) { mu <- c(par[1], par[2]) sigma <- matrix(c(par[3], par[4], par[4], par[5]), nrow = 2) -sum(dmvnorm(dat, mean = mu, sigma = sigma, log = T)) } tryCatch(optim(par = c(1, 1, 3, 1, 5), fn = like_fun, lower = c(-Inf, -Inf, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1), method = "L-BFGS-B"), error = function(e) print("The covariance matrix is not positive definite")) ## $par ## [1] 0.9675064 3.9193232 3.1357536 1.9141789 4.9587980 ## ## $value ## [1] 4075.551 ## ## $counts ## function gradient ## 16 16 ## ## $convergence ## [1] 0 ## ## $message ## [1] "CONVERGENCE: REL_REDUCTION_OF_F <= FACTR*EPSMCH" #if the matrix created isn't positive definite, then this will break Returning to mixed models Suppose optim() gives us one specific set of parameter values: par <- oo$par gamma <- par[1] beta <- par[2] tau2 <- par[3] sigma2 <- par[4] Right now, we are not optimizing. We are simply asking: If these were the true parameter values, how likely would our observed data be? To answer that, we must compute the likelihood of the data under this model. Step 1: Compute the Predicted Mean The fixed-effects part of our model is pred_fixed_effect <- gamma + beta * ss$days This is exactly what we would compute in ordinary regression. So far, nothing new. This gives us the predicted mean reaction time for each observation. Step 2: Why We Cannot Multiply Independent Densities In ordinary regression, we assume the observations are independent. That means the likelihood is just: Multiply one normal density for each observation. But in a random intercept model, observations from the same subject share the same random intercept. That means: Observations from the same subject are correlated. Observations from different subjects are independent. So we cannot multiply independent densities anymore. Instead, we must use a multivariate normal distribution that accounts for correlation. ** Step 3: Build the Grouping Matrix** We create a factor indicating subject membership: g <- factor(ss$subject) Z <- model.matrix(~ 0 + g) Z ## It creates an ( N N ) matrix where: Entries are 1 if two observations belong to the same subject. Entries are 0 otherwise. So this matrix marks which observations share a random intercept. 9.1.2 What does multiplying by tau2 do? It says: If two observations belong to the same subject, their covariance is ( ^2 ). This creates correlation within each subject. 9.1.3 What does sigma2 * diag(N) do? This adds residual variance to the diagonal. That ensures that: Each observation has total variance ( ^2 + ^2 ). Only observations from the same subject share covariance. 9.1.4 What does the final matrix represent? The matrix V contains: Diagonal entries: total variance of each observation Off-diagonal entries within a subject: shared variance ( ^2 ) Off-diagonal entries across subjects: 0 So V encodes the entire correlation structure of the data. This is the key difference between regression and mixed models. Step 5: Evaluate the Multivariate Normal Density Finally, we compute: dmvnorm(ss$reaction, mean = pred_fixed_effect, sigma = V, log = TRUE) ## [1] -897.4195 This computes the log-likelihood of the entire response vector at once. Instead of multiplying many independent normal densities, we now evaluate one multivariate normal density that accounts for: The mean structure The within-subject correlation That single number is: The log-likelihood of the data under this parameter choice. In ordinary regression: Build the mean. Assume constant variance. Multiply independent normal densities. In a mixed model: Build the mean. Carefully construct a covariance matrix that reflects the random effects. Evaluate one multivariate normal density. The hardest part is building the covariance matrix correctly. Once that is done, the rest is just plugging into the multivariate normal formula. par <- oo$par library(mvtnorm) nll <- function(par) { gamma <- par[1] beta <- par[2] tau2 <- par[3] sigma2 <- par[4] if (tau2 < 0 || sigma2 <= 0) return(Inf) response <- ss$reaction pred_fixed_effect <- gamma + beta * ss$days #this is the same as mu, which is a good check g <- factor(ss$subject) #this is the grouping variable for the random intercepts) Z <- model.matrix(~ 0 + g) # columns correspond to groups (levels of g) N <- length(response) V <- tau2 * (Z %*% t(Z)) + sigma2 * diag(N) # Marginal covariance: V = tau2 * Z Z' + sigma2 * I_N -dmvnorm(response, mean = pred_fixed_effect, sigma = V, log = TRUE) } nll(par) ## [1] 897.4195 optim(par = par, fn = nll, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(-Inf, -Inf, 0, 0)) ## $par ## [1] 251.40703 10.46715 1379.07124 954.27973 ## ## $value ## [1] 897.0538 ## ## $counts ## function gradient ## 15 15 ## ## $convergence ## [1] 0 ## ## $message ## [1] "CONVERGENCE: REL_REDUCTION_OF_F <= FACTR*EPSMCH" summary(mod_lmer) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: reaction ~ days + (1 | subject) ## Data: ss ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 1786.5 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -3.2257 -0.5529 0.0109 0.5188 4.2506 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## subject (Intercept) 1378.2 37.12 ## Residual 960.5 30.99 ## Number of obs: 180, groups: subject, 18 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. The data seems pretty good to me, but I can see where some people didn’t think so. As long as you say why. Exercise 2.3 Note that \(\sum_{i = 1}^n \beta_0 = n\beta_0\). The solution is \(\hat \beta_0 = \overline{y} - \overline{x}\). \(\hat \beta_0\) is normal with mean \(\beta_0\) and variance \(\sigma^2/n\). Let’s simulate. xs <- runif(20, 0, 10) sim_data <- replicate(10000, { ys <- 2 + xs + rnorm(20, 0, 1) mean(ys) - mean(xs) }) plot(density(sim_data)) curve(dnorm(x, 2, 1/sqrt(20)), add = T, col = 2) Exercise 2.4 We have that \[ \frac{\hat \beta_1 - \beta_1}{\sqrt{nS^2/(n\sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2)}} \sim t_{n -2} \] So we compute. dd <- HistData::Galton mod <- lm(child ~ parent, data = dd) summary(mod) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = child ~ parent, data = dd) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -7.8050 -1.3661 0.0487 1.6339 5.9264 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) ## (Intercept) 23.94153 2.81088 8.517 <2e-16 *** ## parent 0.64629 0.04114 15.711 <2e-16 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ## ## Residual standard error: 2.239 on 926 degrees of freedom ## Multiple R-squared: 0.2105, Adjusted R-squared: 0.2096 ## F-statistic: 246.8 on 1 and 926 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 The estimate for \(S\) is given as 2.239, which we use. We compute the test statistic: (0.64629 - 1)/sqrt(2.239^2/(sum(dd$parent^2) - 1/928 * sum(dd$parent)^2)) ## [1] -8.596837 The test statistic is -8.596837. We need to compute the likelihood of obtaining something that unlikely given that \(H_0\) is true. pt(-8.596837, 926) * 2 ## [1] 3.454205e-17 With this \(p\)-value, we reject the null hypothesis. We conlcude that the slope is not 1. With more work, we can see that this means (roughly) that parents who are short or tall will tend to have children that are again short or tall, but less so than the parents. Does that mean that eventually there will be little variation among heights of humans. Why or why not? I’ll pull out the test data and leave the train data with the same variable name. test_indices <- sample(1:176, 46) test_dat <- ChemicalManufacturingProcess[test_indices,] ChemicalManufacturingProcess <- ChemicalManufacturingProcess[-test_indices,] The data isn’t in the format that the book said it would be in. Let’s create a matrix of predictors and a vector response, in addition to the data frame with both. predictors <- ChemicalManufacturingProcess[,-1] response <- ChemicalManufacturingProcess[,1] Now let’s see about missing data. sum(is.na(predictors)) ## [1] 88 We do have missing data, so we will need to preprocess. The first part of the problem asks us to do Principle Component Regression. Let’s do it using the caret package. library(caret) ## Loading required package: ggplot2 ## Loading required package: lattice train(x = predictors, y = response, method = "pcr", preProcess = c("center", "scale", "medianImpute", "nzv")) ## Principal Component Analysis ## ## 130 samples ## 57 predictor ## ## Pre-processing: centered (56), scaled (56), median imputation (56), remove (1) ## Resampling: Bootstrapped (25 reps) ## Summary of sample sizes: 130, 130, 130, 130, 130, 130, ... ## Resampling results across tuning parameters: ## ## ncomp RMSE Rsquared MAE ## 1 1.923932 0.2143977 1.453886 ## 2 1.931708 0.2811579 1.376702 ## 3 2.100334 0.2650185 1.393008 ## ## RMSE was used to select the optimal model using the smallest value. ## The final value used for the model was ncomp = 1. I think we need to expand our tune grid a bit. tuneGrid <- data.frame(ncomp = 1:20) pca_mod <- train(x = predictors, y = response, method = "pcr", tuneGrid = tuneGrid, preProcess = c("center", "scale", "medianImpute", "nzv")) apply(pca_mod$results[,c(2, 5)], 1, sum) ## 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 ## 2.538925 2.217215 2.620412 2.848612 3.369809 3.308128 3.522237 3.580313 ## 9 10 11 12 13 14 15 16 ## 3.180316 3.338443 3.340587 3.059151 3.000264 2.828649 2.497024 2.321957 ## 17 18 19 20 ## 2.285783 2.486719 2.498090 2.882467 The smallest value 1 se away from the estimated MSE is 2.2172154. So, by our one se rule of them, we will choose ncomp <- which(pca_mod$results[,2] < min(apply(pca_mod$results[,c(2, 5)], 1, sum))) ncomp <- min(ncomp) ncomp ## [1] 1 This says that we need one component, and our estimate for the MSE is roughly \(2.1 \pm .92\). pca_mod$results[1,2] ## [1] 2.07493 pca_mod$results[1,5] ## [1] 0.4639948 Let’s check it out on our test set that we haven’t touched yet.
